articleHeadline: Marburg Virus: Symptoms, Causes, Diagnosis, and Treatment
articleSummary: Marburg virus disease is a deadly, rare hemorrhagic fever caused by Marburgvirus. Symptoms start with fever, malaise, and body aches and can progress to severe bleeding and organ failure. First identified in 1967 after outbreaks in Germany and Serbia linked to a shipment of infected African green monkeys from Uganda, causing seven deaths. Outbreaks have occurred in Uganda, Angola, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Kenya, Guinea, Equatorial Guinea, Ghana, and Tanzania. Transmission occurs from animals to humans—primarily via African fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus) in caves or mines—and between people through body fluids or contaminated objects; sexual transmission via semen may occur weeks after recovery. Incubation ranges 2 days to 3 weeks; symptoms typically appear about a week after infection. Fatality ranges 23-90%, with deaths about 8–9 days after onset. Diagnosis relies on ELISA or PCR; no approved cure exists; prevention relies on PPE and safe handling.

articleHeadline: A lump in the chest wasn't cancer but a 'parasite'... What happened to a woman in her 60s?
articleSummary: 65-year-old woman in the Democratic Republic of the Congo presented with a chest lump that persisted for seven years. Surgical excision and histopathology confirmed subcutaneous cysticercosis due to Taenia solium larvae, with the scolex observed inside the mass. This non-neural manifestation contrasts with neurocysticercosis, and the lesion resembled a soft tissue tumor. Complete removal obviated the need for antiparasitic therapy, and one-year follow-up showed no symptoms. Transmission likely occurs via ingestion of eggs from contaminated food or water or poor hygiene, with fecal-oral spread; emphasis on hand hygiene and sanitary handling of food and water. articleHeadline: Measles can trigger an ear infection.
articleSummary: Brazil reports new measles cases in 2026 after November 2024 recertification of elimination of endemic transmission. Measles can trigger acute otitis media, an ear infection that may cause temporary or permanent hearing loss. Dr. Naiara Amorim of HOPE notes that measles causes intense respiratory inflammation and temporary immune suppression, creating a milieu for bacterial middle-ear infection. Inflammation can block the Eustachian tube, trapping fluids in the middle ear and enabling bacterial growth. Typical symptoms include intense ear pain, fever, malaise, and a feeling of fullness; in babies, irritability, persistent crying, sleep difficulties, feeding refusal, and ear-pulling. Complications range from conductive hearing loss to potential permanent sensorineural loss; severe cases include tympanic membrane perforation and mastoiditis, and in rare instances meningitis. Prevention emphasizes vaccination: MMR; pneumococcal, meningococcal vaccines; and influenza vaccination to reduce respiratory infections. Early diagnosis and medical evaluation are key, particularly if symptoms persist after measles infection.

articleHeadline: Breakbone fever on the rise due to El Niño
articleSummary: Breakbone fever (dengue) is poised for a surge as a record-breaking El Niño coincides with a global dengue spread. El Niño has been linked to about 63% of annual dengue fluctuations; major events (1982/83, 1997/98, 2015/16, 2023/24) preceded large outbreaks, with 2023/24 estimated 9.6 million additional infections. Brazil faces a potential rise in dengue, chikungunya, and Zika; Fiocruz projects up to about 1.7 million dengue cases in 2027. Taiwan recalls 2015 with 43,000 cases and 228 deaths. Four dengue serotypes mean prior infection offers incomplete protection; a secondary infection with a different serotype can raise severe disease risk. Preparedness: education, eliminating standing water, vector control, Wolbachia trials, vaccination when available, and hospital early-warning systems.

articleHeadline: Ticks, vectors of dangerous diseases; five patients in Thailand have died.
articleSummary: Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) is a tick-borne viral illness. During 2025-2026, Thailand surveillance recorded six confirmed SFTS cases with five deaths, including two in Phetchabun Province, Northern Thailand. SFTSV has been detected in ticks from the area, including dog ticks. Transmission is mainly by infected tick bites, with possible spread through contact with blood or secretions of infected animals or people. Incubation is about 5-14 days, with fever, fatigue, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and sometimes altered consciousness. Lab findings include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and abnormal liver or kidney function; severe cases may progress to acute kidney injury, myocarditis, arrhythmias, meningitis, or encephalitis. Pet owners should regularly check pets for ticks, use preventive products, avoid handling ticks bare-handed, and minimize exposure to sick animals' blood. Outdoor workers should wear protective clothing, use repellent, check for ticks after outdoor activity, and seek care if fever or tick bite occurs.
